title: Rashi on Chullin
text: 'מתני MISHNA: Everyone slaughters - Everywhere that [the tanna] teaches "everyone," in each instance he brings the halacha from the beginning of tractate Arakhin and explains (Arakh. 2a:4), "Everyone [makes valuations], to include whom?" And "everyone slaughters," which is taught in the Mishna, the amoraim argue about it in the Gemara to [ultimately] say, "to include an impure person [slaughtering an animal] for mundane use," and to say, "to include a Samaritan or a heretic."
וכולן And all of them - In the Gemara it is explained who are "and all of them."

GEMARA: 'And their slaughter is valid' after the fact - This [should be read as] a question [rather than a statement] (i.e., "And [is the Mishna saying that] their slaughter is valid after the fact?"). And the opening clause ("Everyone may slaughter") is difficult, for it implies that whoever is included in "everyone" is included ab initio. But if the latter clause ("and their slaughter is valid") implies that it is extending [the same meaning of] "everyone," then it would be extending [the same] to [encompass] an after-the-fact [slaughter], but we do not extend [the authorization to perform an act] ab initio [to encompass what is only acceptable] after the fact. And thus we cannot say that our Mishnah withholds something ab initio and that [only] one [thing] is taught. For since it is taught "Everyone may slaughter," it would be obvious that [their slaughter is] valid! [This would render the latter clause redundant.]

וכל And does every [use of the word] "everyone" (הכל) indicate [that the action may be performed] ab initio? - [For if you take that position,] it would be difficult for you [to explain all similar instances where הכל is used]. Nor would you be able to say that every [instance indicates that the action is valid] after the fact. And this is what the tanna means to say: "Everyone as to whom the laws of slaughter apply [may slaughter]." For [otherwise], if those who were disqualified from slaughtering [nonetheless] slaughtered, it would come out that their slaughter was valid [after the fact]. [This result would be unacceptable.]

אלא Rather, "Everyone (הכל) may substitute [an unconsecrated animal for a consecrated animal]" (Tem. 1:1) - Can it be [seriously] claimed that this statement is [intended to authorize that] ab initio, one may bring an unconsecrated animal in place of a consecrated animal, and say, "This one is a substitute for that one"?! [Certainly not! Rather,] the "everyone" in [the tractate of] Temurah is explained over there (Tem. 2a:6-8) to include an heir who substitutes the offering of his [deceased] father, and it is taught over there, that one may not substitute with the offering of another.
טוב Good - Unblemished.
רע Bad - Blemished.

התם Over there, the tanna means to say - To uproot the "everyone" stated in the first clause (i.e., of Temurah 1:1), so as not to say that it means "ab initio." But "everyone slaughters" remains in its place, since as long as he does not uproot it, and teaches that disqualified individuals should not be permitted to slaughter, [then he can argue by analogy that] in the same way that it is uprooted over there from the implication [that the rule of substitutions applies] ab initio, he extends it, and thereafter he teaches "and their slaughter is valid," so that it implies [validity] after the fact.

לא שהאדם רשאי Not that a person is permitted - It is written (Lev. 27:10), "He shall not substitute for it [and he shall not exchange it]," and the first clause [of Tem. 1:1] means to say the following: "Everyone as to whom the laws of substitution apply..." And thus it is taught that the first clause, "Everyone substitutes," is necessary (see Tem. 2b:5). Also, [the clause is necessary] to explain "not that a person is permitted [ab initio], etc.," and he did not state in the first clause [due to the] abbreviated phrasing [of the Mishna], "Everyone who substituted, their substitutions are [valid] substitutions." This is the wording of the tannaim, such as "Everyone slaughters," "Everyone leans [their hands on an offering]," "Everyone is obligated." Therefore, here, even though [the tanna] had a need to lengthen [his wording], the tanna did not wish to alter his wording.
מומר It is a [valid] exchange - Liability is incurred for the second [animal], and both of them (i.e., both animals involved in the substitution) are [deemed] consecrated.
וסופג He incurs forty lashes - On account of the negative commandment of, "he shall not exchange it" (Lev. 27:10).

הכל מעריכין Everyone may make valuations - Over there (Arakh. 2a:4), it is explained to include a [minor] of uncertain ability to discriminate [in matters of valuations], who is close in age to adulthood; a child who knows how to clearly utter [a vow of valuation] in the name of those who are consecrating; and if he is next to his parent, he is [considered to be] like one who is twelve years and one day old, [and] his words are established [as binding] even though they know that he is a minor, until he is thirteen years and one day old.

מעריכין May make valuations - The laws of valuations apply to them, for if he said, "It is incumbent upon me to donate my valuation," or "The valuation of so-and-so is incumbent upon me," his vow is established. And even though he is a minor, the person who took the vow is liable to give double the valuation, and amount is fixed on the portion [of valuations in the Torah (Lev. 27:3-7)].

הכל נערכין All are valuated - They have a valuation, and even one who is afflicted with boils [to the extent] that he would be worth nothing if he were sold in the marketplace, his valuation is [fixed by] the portion [of valuations in the Torah], and if he said concerning himself, "It is incumbent upon me to donate my valuation," or he said about another, "The valuation of that one who is afflicted with boils is incumbent upon me," they do not say [to him], "Since he has no market value, he also has no valuation." [Rather, his valuation is set by the Torah irrespective of his true market value, and the one who vowed is liable to fulfill his obligation.]

הכל נודרים All may vow - "My market-value is incumbent upon me" or "The market-value of so-and-so is incumbent upon me." And over there (Arakh. 2a:4) it is explained, that since [the tanna] wanted to teach "All may be the subject of a vow," he also taught "All may vow."

הכל נידרין All may be the subject of a vow - Every person who has no worth [nevertheless] has a market-value, and if he said "My market-value is incumbent upon me," or another said about him, "The market-value of so-and-so is incumbent upon me," he gives according to what he is sold for in the marketplace, and even if he was vowed for less than a one-month old, and he said "The market-value of this infant is incumbent upon me," he gives his market-value, and even though there is no assessment-value [under Torah law] less than that of a one-month old. Or if he said [regarding the newborn infant], "His assessment-value is incumbent upon me," he is exempt from everything, for the law of assessment-values was not given for him, as it is written (Lev. 27:6), "And if from the age of one month up to the age of five years...."
לא There shall not be any sin in it - Here, if you were to vow, there would be [an element of] sin it.

טוב אשר Better than one who did not vow - Before that (i.e., that which was quoted) it is written "...one who vows [and] pays, and even the best of all is one who does not vow [in the first place], lest he vows and does not pay." This is how Rabbi Meir explains it.
טוב מזה Better than this one and that one - Than one who vows and pays and who vows and does not pay.
שאינו Who does not vow whatsoever - For one who accustoms himself to making vows comes to eventually not fulfill his words.

רבי יהודה Rabbi Yehuda says, better than this one and that one is one who vows and pays - The implication here is that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay, but one who vows and pays -- is he not better than all of them?

ואפילו And even Rabbi Yehuda only said so in relation to one who says, "Behold, this [animal is hereby consecrated]" - For if it dies or is stolen, he is not liable for it responsibility. Alternatively, since it can be brought out to pasture [until it develops a blemish], he can go back on it (i.e., a that point he may treat the animal as chullin without having broken his vow).

אבל But [if] he said "It is incumbent upon me," no - Perhaps he will transgress and fail to fulfill [his vow], and thus it is established in the first chapter of Nedarim (Ned. 10a:1-2), for Rabbi Yehuda teaches "[best of all] is one who volunteers [a freewill offering] and pays (משלם)." (Note: This is a paraphrase of Nedarim, where the Gemara uses the term "מקיים" ("fulfills") rather than "משלם" ("pays").) Therefore, are "[everyone] may make valuations" and "[everyone] may vow" ab initio? No. For "[i]t is incumbent upon me" cannot be said [to be included] in it.
וכל And does every "everyone" (הכל) [indicate that the act is] not [authorized] ab initio? - Is there nowhere that "everyone" does not [mean] ab initio?
הכל חייבים בסוכה Everyone is obligated in Sukkah - To include a minor who does not need his mother (see Arakh. 2b:4).
הכל חייבים בציצית Everyone is obligated in tzitzit - To include a minor who knows how to wrap himself [in the tzitzit] (see Arakh. 2b:6).
חייבין I am not speaking about "obligated" - Where it teaches "obligated," it is certainly obvious that [the tanna] is speaking [in terms of performance] ab initio.

הכל סומכין Everyone leans [on an offering] - To include an heir, and this is certainly speaking [in terms of performance] of ab initio, for [in connection with] a commandment, they [would even] impose [the obligation] upon him against his will.

תרתי Why do I need two [phrases to teach] after the fact? - The Mishna should have been taught as follows: "The slaughter of everyone is valid [after the fact], except for that of a deaf-mute, and imbecile, and a minor." [Had it done so,] it would properly be implied that those who are included in "everyone" after the fact, are included, but not [that they have the right to slaughter] ab initio. Alternatively, it should have taught, "Everyone may slaughter" separately (i.e., omitting "and their slaughter is valid"), as it is taught elsewhere, "[everyone] may make vows of valuation" and "[everyone] may vow" without [further] explaining, "Why do I need [the Mishnah] to teach this?" [Rather,] "everyone may slaughter" is necessary in order to explain "and their slaughter is valid," to say that those who [are included in] "slaughter" in the opening phrase [are only considered valid to slaughter] after the fact. And if that is difficult [for you], in Temurah it is also taught in this way, and it is explained over there. It is not taught in that case, "All may substitute, and their substitutions are [valid] substitutions," next to each other. And if it is because of, "Not that a person is permitted" (Tem. 2a:2), but in the event that one may come to engage in such a [forbidden] act, that he would be subject to forty lashes, to teach us that one is administered lashes on account of [violating] a negative commandment [even] where no physical action is [involved] in it.

הכי קתני This is how it should be taught - [Both] ab initio and after the fact, to teach us "everyone may slaughter" ab initio to include an impure person [who slaughters an animal] for unconsecrated use.
פשיטא That is obvious! - For Israelites were not warned about [any need to] maintain ritual purity for their unconsecrated food.

שנעשו That were prepared with the ritual purity of consecrated food - For he accepted upon himself [the stringencies of] eating with the ritual purity [reserved for those who partake of] consecrated food, for he wanted to accustom himself to [maintaining] the ritual purity of consecrated food, for if he were to eat peace-offerings or thanksgiving-offerings, he would be an expert in observing those [stringencies].

כקדש דמו Like that of consecrated food - And he is required to separate [himself] according to rabbinic law from all disqualifying impurities. And nevertheless (i.e., if he nevertheless became impure), [he may slaughter] ab initio, and with a long knife (i.e., to avoid contaminating the carcass by touch after the slaughter), as it is explained (Hul. 2b:8).

ובמוקדשין And regarding consecrated [animals] - Ab initio, [one who is impure] may not slaughter, even with a long knife, since he is warned from the Torah that he must not cause [a sacrifice] to become impure, as it is written (Num. 18:8), "Behold I have given over to you the guarding of my terumah-gifts[, and all the consecrated things of the Children of Israel, etc.]." Wherefore, in regards to the of "guarding," our Rabbis decreed that [an impure person may not slaughter] ab initio on account of [the maxim], "Go, go, we say to a Nazirite. Go around, go around, [but] do not come near to the vineyard" (Avodah Zarah 17a:6).

שחיטתן כשרה His slaughter is valid - For we had [to account for] the after-the-fact [language] from the Mishna. And below it explains how it can be [that an impure] person does not defile the knife, and then goes back and defiles the meat itself (i.e., through the knife) (see Hul. 3a:1-2).
גרידי Only [unconsecrated animals] - For he did not accept upon himself [the stringencies of performing mundane slaughter with] the purity of a priest.
שמא ישהו Lest they interrupt [the slaughter] - And it would be rendered a neveilah, as is taught in the Mishna throughout the second chapter.

דיעבד נמי [The slaughter] is also not valid after the fact lest they interrupt [the slaughter] - It is explained why this is the holding: Lest they will come to ruin [the slaughter]. In the Mishna, it (i.e., יְקַלְקְלוּ -- they will come to ruin) is taught in future tense, in order to teach that [other Jews] may not hand over unconsecrated [animals] to them ab initio, and even [if] others are watching over them, they warn them that [the slaughter] will always come to ruin.

דעלה קאי It stands adjacent - It [therefore] removes them (i.e., the deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor). What, then, is implied by "and all of those"? It also comes to teach that there are others [who are included in the rule], for [if it meant to refer back to the deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor] it should have taught, "and if they slaughtered."

ואלא אטמא במוקדשין And perhaps [the Mishna is referring to] an impure person [slaughtering] sacrificial [animals] - You have said that the Mishna is speaking of [a situation where someone] is told, "Do not slaughter." Why, then, discuss [an impure person slaughtering sacrificial animals] specifically [in regards to] "and others watch him"? Haven't you already said that his [testimony] is believed if he said, "It is clear to me [that I did not touch the carcass after the slaughter]"?
They are mentally crafty – like the first human; but they consider themselves as animals, lowly in spirit.
Ginai: The name of the river.
The will of my Maker: All the streams flow to the sea by decree of the King.
It is uncertain [whether you] will perform: Lest they not give you [the captives] for the ransom.

As he is engaged in the commandment: As it is written (Exodus 12:17), "You must guard the matzot" - as [the wheat] requires guarding for the sake of the matzah from the time of the grinding and the sifting.
Who was with them: He attached himself to them on the journey.
Tayya: An Arab merchant.
That is what one does: By way of a question.
To those who accompany as part of the group. We leave them and go?
Perhaps here too, one time: Rather he was afraid, lest the waters return and flush down the [other] two. So he was speaking to the [water], that the river should wait for them.
As Moses and the six hundred thousand for whom the Red Sea had parted.

They threw it down: They threw it down in a sieve to clean it. Vaner in [Old French]. And it should not be said that it is an expression of threshing, such that it was at first in its shells. As, if so, why did it not eat it at first? Behold, it did not become obligated for tithing until it is flattened on the threshing floor, as it is written (Deuteronomy 18:4), "The beginning of your grain." And it is taught explicitly (Peah 1:6), "One may feed domestic beasts, wild animals and birds [and be exempt from tithes] until he flattens (the threshing floor)." For any eating of animals is considered a casual eating (which is exempt from tithing).
They separated it manually from the stones and the chaff.

And is one obligated: Did they at all decree demai on animal food purchased from an ignoramus? And even though if [the seller] certainly did not tithe it, [the buyer] would be obligated to tithe it; it was not decreed, however, when there is [only] a doubt. As it was taught, "One who purchases [grain in the market] for sowing or for feeding an animal" - even though seeds and animal food are included with all grain and are obligated for tithing - they did not decree demai upon them. As, in general, most ignoramuses tithe, so the Sages were not so stringent about demai.
For hides to process them.
And it is taught: By way of a statement. And they initially bought this barley for a person.
Rabbi heard that Rabbi Pinchas was coming.
Your desire is to dine with me: Is it your desire to dine with me?
His face beamed: He was happy, since Rabbi Pinchas was not accustomed to benefitting from that which belonged to others - as per the below.
He said to him - Rabbi Pinchas - "And did you hold that deriving benefit from the Jewish people is forbidden to me by vow."
The Jewish people are holy: So it is fitting to derive benefit from them.
But there is one who wants to give benefit from what is his to others, but he does not have the ability in his hands. So I do not want to derive benefit from him, so that I do not burden him.

And there is one who has the ability in his hands to give benefit to others; yet even though he says, "Come and dine," his heart does not desire [it]. So I do not benefit from him on account of it being written, "Eat not the bread of him that has an evil eye."
Eat not the bread: Do not dine. Bread is a term for a meal, as it is written (I Samuel 20:27), "did not come [...] to the bread"; and it is written (Daniel 5:1), "King Belshazzar made a great bread."
As one who has reckoned (shaar): It is as if you open a gate (shaar) in his stomach. But some say it is a term of bitterness, as in (Jeremiah 29:17), "like bitter (shoerim) figs."
I am rushing (mesarheivna): It is an expression of frenzy and quickness. That is to say, I need to hurry and go to a matter involving a commandment, so I have no time to dine.
Kudneita: Mules, and they belonged to Rabbi.
The Angel of Death: Once it strikes, the wound cannot heal, as per the below.

And before the blind, etc.: As just like they are forbidden to you, so too are they forbidden to others. And behold it cannot be said that he would sell them to idolaters, as we learned (Avodah Zarah 14b), "We may not sell them a large domesticated beast."
I will declare them ownerless: I will send them away into any of the forests to be ownerless.
You will thereby increase the damage: As since they will not be guarded, they will increase their damage.
I will remove: So that they will not be able to kick. And there is no [violation of], 'do not destroy' - as they would [still] be fit for threshing.
I will remove: He would remove their hooves, but they would still be able to walk.
Mevatash: Plead. And its colleague (another example) is in Shevuot (30b). We teach the version, mevatash, with a [letter], , and not with a kaf.
A mountain rose between them and separated them.

During their lifetimes - of the righteous - the Holy One, blessed He, pays attention to their desires, so as not to change their minds. For He caused this thing, that he should enter by the gate of the mules, so that he separate and not change his mind from at first, as it is was not his way to dine from that which belonged to others - as per the below.
All the more so: As behold, they are greater [after] their death than in the their lifetimes, as Rabbi Chama said.
They were burying a man: He was a wicked man, and he should not have been buried next to the righteous.

And as soon as the man touched the bones of Elisha, he revived: Yet in his lifetime, when he wanted to revive the son of the Shunamite woman, he needed to place his mouth over his mouth and his eyes over his eyes and request mercy.

And perhaps it was to fulfill the blessing of Eliyahu: For it would be insufficient if it was not fulfilled; as it is written about the righteous (Job 22:28), "You will decree and it will be fulfilled." So it was not for the sake of Elisha.
A double portion: Eliyahu revived the son of the Tzarfit woman and Elisha revived the son of the Shunamite woman. So he needed to revive still another.
If so: In order to fulfill the blessing of Eliyahu.

This is that which was taught: By way of a question. And if it was for the sake of Eliyahu's blessing, he should have truly revived him, like the one that Eliyahu revived. Rather is it not that we understand from it that it was for the sake of Elisha. And Elisha only needed to remove him from being next to him. So he revived him until he was removed from there.
Please, let her not be as one dead: This is written about the tzaraat (skin ailment) of Miriam.
Why are their names called - of the mules - yemim, as it is written (Genesis 36:24), "who found the yemim."
None have asked me: Rabbi Chanina was a physician. And in Tractate Yoma (49a:10) in [the chapter entitled] Hotziu Lo, they bring it from here (that he was a physician).
And survive: It is implied that the one struck dies.
And healed: [The verb] is in the feminine, and it is referring to the wound (and not the man), as the wound does not heal.
There is none else beside Him: This is mentioned for on account of Rabbi Chanina (since he was just mentioned above).
Even sorcery is not beside Him, meaning to say, without His will. For if there is no decree upon a man, evil cannot be done to him.
Try: She was trying and applying herself that he not [notice].
To take dust and to do sorcery to him and to kill him.
Keshafim: It is an anagram: Makchishim pamaliya shel maalah (Contradicting the retinue of the Above). As they did not decree about this man, that he should die through sorcery.
Nokef: Hurt; acoper in [Old French].
They declare: They decree about him.
Appeases: Atones.
Right thumb: Since it is hurt with power, so that one experiences much pain.
With regard to a second wound before the first wound is healed.
Broke [bread]: The blessing of HaMotzi (over bread). As he did not want to eat [even] the measure of an olive (kazayit) from that of others.
It is forbidden to eat cheese - Because meat exudes fat that stays in the mouth and the taste stays in the mouth.

Mishna: A drop of dairy that falls upon a piece [of meat] - Inside the pot upon one piece [of meat among several] and it the pot is not stirred; it [the pot] will not acquire the taste of the drop, rather only the piece by itself.

If it [the drop of dairy] gives taste to a piece [of meat] - that is to say; [if] the piece of meat by itself is not 60 times larger, to nullify the drop, the piece is immediately forbidden.  And the remaining pieces in the pot are not discussed by the Tanna of our Mishna.  The Gemara argues if the piece returns and makes [all pieces] forbidden or not.
Stir the pot - Stir it immediately before the piece [of meat] receives taste from the drop [of dairy] because it will have been stirred, the drop, with everything.
If there is a drop of taste into the pot - That is to say; the drop has no strength to make everything forbidden, unless it gives taste to the whole pot.
That if you should think - in all other prohibitions [deriving from] its taste are from the rabbis ["derabanan"] and we do not learn them from [the Torah prohibition against] milk in meat.

Rav said - This is because we learned in the Mishnah "if a drop of milk falls on a slice of meat and imparts a flavor to it" it invalidates the whole pot, since that piece itself becomes entirely prohibited and prohibits the other pieces. Even if they consist of [enough volume] to nullify [the drop], they are all prohibited.
Because they are the same type of substance - Rav holds like Rabbi Yehuda who said that min b'mino does not nullify.
In a thick broth - [with] finely [cut] meat [throughout], and fat [in it], such that the entire [broth] is [considered] a type of meat.
2 Sweep away evil - It is a mitzvah for all who are obligated in the death penalty to brought before the beit din so that evil is swept out of Israel
